intro: Wet rooms have become one of the most popular bathroom upgrades in Easthouses over the past few years, and it's easy to see why. A properly installed wet room transforms a cramped or dated bathroom into a sleek, fully waterproofed shower space that's easier to clean, more accessible, and genuinely adds value to your home. But getting one installed correctly is not a straightforward job — it demands careful tanking, precise drainage placement, and a thorough understanding of your existing floor structure. In Easthouses, where the housing stock ranges from solid stone-built homes to newer estate properties, the approach needs to be tailored carefully to what's already there.
localContext: Easthouses presents a genuinely mixed picture when it comes to wet room installations. The older stone-built properties and period cottages that make up a good portion of the town's housing tend to have solid concrete or timber suspended floors, both of which require very different preparation before any tanking membrane goes down. Timber floors in older homes often need reinforcement or replacement sections before they can support the weight and moisture demands of a wet room — skip this step and you're looking at a failed installation within a couple of years. The modern estate homes in Easthouses are generally more straightforward to work with, but they come with their own considerations around lightweight partitioning and underfloor heating compatibility. Easthouses sits in a moderately hard water area, which is worth bearing in mind when selecting your fixtures — hard water deposits can affect shower heads, screens, and chrome fittings over time, so specifying appropriate materials and considering a inline scale reducer is a sensible precaution that a good local installer will raise with you.
serviceDetail: A wet room installation in Easthouses typically follows a clear sequence of stages, though the timeline and complexity vary depending on your property. The first step is a thorough survey of the existing bathroom — assessing the floor construction, checking the fall and drainage options, and identifying where the waste will run. In older stone-built homes in Easthouses, this survey stage is especially important because surprises under the floor are common. Once the scope is agreed, strip-out begins: removing the existing suite, floor coverings, and sometimes sections of screed or boarding. Next comes the structural preparation — levelling, reinforcing timber floors where needed, or building up a former to create the correct gradient towards the drain. Tanking is then applied across the entire floor and walls to a minimum height, usually with a liquid applied membrane system or a sheet membrane depending on the substrate. This waterproofing stage is where wet rooms succeed or fail, and it should never be rushed. Wall boards or tiles go on next, followed by the drain, shower valve, and any glass screens or fixed glass panels. A quality installation in Easthouses will typically take between five and eight working days from strip-out to a finished, usable wet room, though more complex older properties can run longer.
pricing: In Easthouses, wet room installations typically run from around £6,000 at the lower end for a straightforward conversion in a modern estate property up to £12,000 or more for larger bathrooms or older stone-built homes requiring significant floor preparation and high-specification finishes. The biggest variables are floor structure (timber floors needing reinforcement add cost), the quality of tiles and fixtures chosen, whether underfloor heating is being incorporated, and how complex the drainage route is. A mid-range wet room in a typical Easthouses home with good quality tiling and a quality thermostatic valve will usually sit in the £7,500–£9,500 range. Always get a fixed-price quote after a proper in-person survey — avoid any installer who quotes without seeing the floor.
whyLocal: Choosing a tradesperson who knows Easthouses and the surrounding Midlothian area genuinely matters for a job like this. Local installers will have worked in the same mix of stone-built cottages, older semis, and modern estate homes that make up the town, so they're not guessing when it comes to what's likely under your bathroom floor. They'll also have established relationships with local suppliers, which can help with lead times on materials. And practically speaking, if anything needs attention after the job is done, a local business is easier to get back — accountability matters on a premium installation where the waterproofing has to be right first time.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an older stone-built property in Easthouses?
faqs.a: Yes, absolutely — but it requires more preparation than a modern home. Older properties in Easthouses often have solid floors that need careful assessment, or timber floors that need reinforcing. A proper survey before any work starts is essential. Done correctly, older stone-built homes can make excellent wet rooms with the right waterproofing approach.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation take in Easthouses?
faqs.a: Most wet room installations in Easthouses take between five and eight working days for a standard bathroom. Older properties with more complex floor structures or larger rooms can take up to ten days. Your installer should give you a realistic programme after surveying the space — be wary of anyone promising a very quick turnaround on a full conversion.

faqs.q: Will hard water in Easthouses cause problems with my wet room?
faqs.a: Easthouses is in a moderately hard water area, which won't cause serious problems but can lead to limescale build-up on screens, shower heads, and chrome fittings over time. Specifying a quality shower head with easy-clean nozzles and considering an inline scale reducer are sensible steps. Your installer should flag this and help you choose appropriate fixtures.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for a wet room in Easthouses?
faqs.a: In most cases, no — wet room installations in Easthouses are classed as permitted development and don't require planning permission. If your property is a listed building, which applies to some of the older stone properties in the area, you may need listed building consent before structural alterations. Your installer or local planning office can confirm your specific situation.
